planting.note: Direct sow or set out plugs in spring into dry, sharply-drained sandy or gravelly acidic soil in full sun; this low subshrub naturally colonizes open pine-oak barrens and roadside sand and resents any soil that stays wet.

directions: Canada frostweed forms a low basal rosette of narrow, hairy leaves and sends up wiry stems topped with bright yellow, five-petaled flowers that open for only a few morning hours in late spring before dropping their petals. Later in summer the plant produces a second, inconspicuous crop of small self-pollinating flowers along the stem axils that never open but still set abundant seed, which is the main way it spreads in a garden setting. It is an excellent choice for sandy, infertile, acidic soil where showier perennials struggle, and needs no supplemental water once established. In winter, dried stem bases sometimes extrude delicate curls of ice crystals on the first hard freezes, echoing the larger frost-flower display of its relative Verbesina virginica.

planting.note: Set out container-grown plants in spring into deep, loose, nutrient-poor sand in full sun; golden heather is a true barrens specialist and will rot quickly in any soil that holds organic matter or moisture.

directions: Golden heather forms a low, tangled mat of small evergreen, needle-like leaves on upright gray-green stems, studded in May with bright yellow, broad-petaled flowers that distinguish it from the more silvery, flat-growing Hudsonia tomentosa it often grows alongside. It is native to the open, sun-baked sand of the New Jersey Pine Barrens and other coastal-plain barrens, usually under scattered pitch pine and scrub oak, and depends on excellent drainage and very lean soil to avoid fungal rot. Use it as a textural groundcover in a dedicated sand or gravel garden rather than a conventional border, and avoid fertilizer or irrigation beyond establishment. Specialty native-plant nurseries propagate it from cuttings taken from wild-sourced stock for pine barrens restoration and landscaping projects.

planting.note: Divide clumps or set out plugs in spring into dry, sandy, acidic soil in full sun; this low rosette-forming aster thrives in the same open, nutrient-poor clearings as pitch pine and bearberry and should never be mulched with rich compost.

directions: Sickle-leaved golden aster forms a tight, silvery-haired rosette of narrow, curved leaves that stays attractive year-round in dry sand, sending up short stalks of golden-yellow daisy flowers from late summer into fall when few other pine-barrens natives are still blooming. It is an Atlantic coastal-plain specialty found from Long Island south through the New Jersey Pine Barrens in open, sun-exposed, acidic sand, and makes a durable, low-maintenance edging plant for a native sand or gravel garden. Late-season bees and small butterflies rely on it heavily as a nectar source. It needs no fertilizer and tolerates salt spray and drought once its roots are established.

planting.note: Set divisions or plugs in spring into consistently wet, acidic, sandy-peaty soil at a bog or pond margin in partial shade to full sun; it is well suited to the dappled light along Atlantic white cedar swamp edges and sphagnum seeps.

directions: Virginia marsh St. John's-wort is an upright wetland perennial with pairs of smooth, blue-green leaves and clusters of small pink, five-petaled flowers that open briefly on sunny afternoons in late summer. It grows naturally along the boggy, acidic margins of Pine Barrens ponds and Atlantic white cedar swamps, often in the light shade cast by surrounding shrubs, and needs saturated or standing water at the root zone to thrive. Use it at the wet edge of a rain garden or constructed bog where its pink late-season flowers complement the usual yellow-flowered wetland natives. It spreads slowly by rhizome and rarely needs division more than once every several years.

planting.note: Direct sow or transplant in spring into moist to wet, acidic soil at a pond edge, ditch, or rain garden low point in full sun to partial shade; seedbox tolerates both standing water and periodic drying once established.

directions: Seedbox is an upright branching perennial of pond margins and wet meadows that produces small four-petaled yellow flowers through summer, each quickly giving way to a distinctive cube-shaped seed capsule that persists on the stem through winter and rattles when shaken, a feature that gives the plant its common name. It grows readily along the sunny to lightly shaded, boggy pond shores and roadside ditches typical of the Pine Barrens, making it a good choice for the damp fringe of a rain garden or water feature where its winter seed capsules add structural interest to dried arrangements. It self-sows modestly in consistently moist soil but is not aggressive in a typical garden bed. Cut back old stems in late winter before new growth emerges.

planting.note: Divide corms or set out plugs in spring into dry, sandy, acidic, well-drained soil in full sun; this coastal-plain blazing star grows naturally in the open pine-oak clearings and roadside sand of the Pine Barrens and does poorly in rich or heavy garden loam.

directions: Shaggy blazing star sends up a slender, grass-leaved wand topped by a dense spike of fuzzy, purple-pink flower heads that open from the top downward in late summer and early fall, later than most other garden blazing stars. It is an Atlantic coastal-plain species common in the dry, sandy, acidic clearings of the New Jersey Pine Barrens and provides an important late nectar source for bees and migrating monarch butterflies when little else in the sand barrens is still flowering. Plant it in a lean, sun-baked native bed alongside other barrens species rather than a conventional fertile border, where excess moisture and nutrients cause it to flop and rot. Established corms are long-lived and rarely need division.
